opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because I think the honest answer is that it's been a mixed picture, and the gap between expectations and reality looks different depending on where you sit in the organization.

If you go back a couple of years, right after ChatGPT came out, there was this wave of excitement where every executive was saying, "We need an AI strategy, we need to roll this out everywhere." And a lot of companies did the obvious first thing: they bought seat licenses for a chat assistant, maybe stood up an internal RAG chatbot over their documentation, and expected productivity to just go up across the board. What a lot of them found was that usage was really uneven. You'd have a handful of power users who completely changed how they work, and then a long tail of people who tried it a few times, got a mediocre answer, and went back to their old workflow.

So in that sense, the broad "AI makes everyone 30% more productive overnight" expectation didn't really materialize in the way people hoped. But I don't think that means adoption failed. I think it means the value turned out to be more concentrated than people expected. Where it's really working is in places where the task is well-defined, there's a tight feedback loop, and the output can be checked. Coding is the clearest example. Engineering teams have seen real, measurable changes in how they work, and that's increasingly moving from autocomplete toward agents that can take on whole tasks. Customer support is another one. Some areas of data analysis and internal operations, too.

The other thing that's surprised a lot of people is that the bottleneck usually isn't the model anymore. The models are good enough for a huge range of use cases. The bottleneck is everything around the model: getting the right context to it, integrating with internal systems, figuring out evaluation so you actually know whether it's working, and then the organizational side, like changing processes and getting people to trust it. Companies that treated AI as "buy a tool and hand it out" have been disappointed. Companies that treated it as "redesign a workflow around what this technology is good at" are seeing much more meaningful results.

So I'd say: the near-term expectations were probably overhyped, but I'm actually more optimistic about the long-term impact than I was a few years ago, because we're now seeing what it looks like when it really works, and it's pretty compelling.

r001.rationale: The response describes uneven adoption and says companies redesigning workflows around AI are seeing results, but it does not state that major companies are making AI a core part of their internal operations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly I think the answer is kind of a mixed bag. If you go back a couple of years, the expectation was that basically every company was going to have transformative AI applications in production within, you know, twelve to eighteen months. And what actually happened is that most companies got a lot of prototypes, a lot of demos, a lot of internal hackathon projects, and a much smaller number of things that actually made it into production and are delivering measurable value.

So in that sense, I think it's underdelivered relative to the hype. But I'd push back a little on the framing that it's been a disappointment, because the things that have worked have worked really well. Coding assistants are the obvious example. Customer support is another one. Internal knowledge search, document processing, that kind of thing. Those are real, they're deployed, and in a lot of cases they're changing how people actually do their jobs.

Where I think companies got tripped up is that the hard part was never getting the model to do something impressive once. The hard part is getting it to do the thing reliably, in the context of your messy internal data and your actual workflows, with evaluation in place so you know when it breaks. That's the stuff that looks like boring engineering, and a lot of organizations underinvested in it because the demo made it look easy.

And then the other piece is just organizational. The companies that have done well tend to have someone who really owns the problem end to end, who understands both the business process and what the models can and can't do. The ones that struggled often treated it as a top-down mandate, like "we need an AI strategy," without a clear sense of which problems were actually worth solving.

So my take is the technology is largely living up to expectations. The adoption curve is just slower and lumpier than people predicted, which, if you look at any prior wave of enterprise technology, is exactly what you'd expect.

r001.rationale: The response says some AI applications are deployed and changing how people work, but it does not state that major companies are making AI a core part of their internal operations.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s been slower and messier than a lot of people expected. There was this assumption that once the models got good enough, companies would be able to plug them into their workflows and get a lot of value. But model capability is only one piece of that.

When you actually try to put something into production, you have to figure out how to connect it to your data, how to evaluate whether it’s working, and what happens when it makes a mistake. And then there’s the organizational question: will people change the way they work to use it?

So I’d distinguish between experimentation and adoption. There’s a lot of experimentation, and there are places where people are getting real value. But going from a compelling demo to something that a company relies on every day is still a substantial amount of work. I think the opportunity is there; the timeline just depends on more than how quickly the models improve.

r001.rationale: The response says some places are getting real value, but does not state that major companies are making AI a core part of their internal operations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s been slower and messier than a lot of people expected. There’s a big difference between showing that a model can do something interesting and making it work reliably inside a company’s existing workflow. You have to connect it to the right data, figure out how to measure whether it’s actually doing a good job, and get people comfortable using it.

So I wouldn’t necessarily interpret slower adoption as a lack of value. I think the expectations often underestimated how much work happens around the model. The interesting question is moving from, “Can we build a demo?” to, “Can we give this to somebody and have it consistently make their job easier?” That’s where a lot of the work is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the challenges and slower pace of internal AI adoption, but does not state that major companies are making AI a core part of their operations.
